panels.rationale: Single axial contrast CT of the abdomen from a real patient. Caption and in-text explicitly attribute the image to pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis with air in the intestinal wall, and the CT visibly shows intramural gas in the dilated small bowel loops plus free intraperitoneal air. Both findings map directly to the configured vocabulary; classic radiologic presentation of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis. No age or ethnicity stated; no skin shown; no annotations on the image.

in_text_mentions: The patient presented to the Emergency Department of Nicosia General Hospital with epigastric pain and vomiting during the last five days, without bloody stools. The patient was afebrile, with mild abdominal distention and without peritoneal signs. Leukocytes, amylase, and lactic acid were all within the normal ranges. Abdominal radiograph revealed free air intraperitoneally and abdominal/pelvic computed tomography revealed findings of small bowel ischemic necrosis in the presence of free intraperitoneal air and air in the intestinal wall (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast CT abdomen/pelvis of a real patient post-colonoscopy. Red arrow A indicates bubbly intramural air-filled cystic spaces in the bowel wall (PCI) and red arrow B indicates anterior free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum). Both are classic CT manifestations of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis with associated pneumoperitoneum, directly supported by caption and in-text. The A/B labels are annotations within one CT slice, not separate panels, so the figure is treated as a single panel.

in_text_mentions: Post-procedure CT images showed multiple, thin-walled, air-filled submucosal cysts with evidence of intraperitoneal free air (Figure 3). Given the patient was vitally stable without guarding or rigidity on exam, the decision was made to manage the patient conservatively with monitoring and serial exams. She remained asymptomatic and did not require surgical intervention. She was discharged home and has remained asymptomatic after three months of follow-up.

Identification of PCI may be increasing along with the use of CT in diagnosing abdominal pathology [5]. CT is the ideal imaging modality for diagnosis of PCI, and a classic finding includes intramural gas parallel to the bowel wall (Figure 3) [10,11]. Prior reviews had found PCI to more commonly affect the small intestine, but more recent studies have found a higher incidence in the colon (46%-61.8%), as was seen with our patient [12]. The small intestine is affected in 15.4%-27% of cases, and only in 2.9%-7.0% cases is PCI present in both the colon and small intestine [9,13,14].

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Original coronal CTA of the patient described in this pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis case report; caption explicitly attributes increased bowel pneumatosis to this figure, and the in-text confirms increased pneumoperitoneum with arrows marking the pathology. Bowel dilation is captioned but not in the vocabulary. B: Axial CTA view of the same patient from this pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis case report; caption and in-text directly attribute the bowel pneumatosis and pneumoperitoneum shown (with white arrows) to the target disease. C: Sagittal CTA reconstruction of the same patient; arrows highlight free intraperitoneal gas superiorly and pneumatosis of bowel loops, consistent with the caption and in-text describing increased bowel pneumatosis and pneumoperitoneum in this case report.

in_text_mentions: between the patient’s mostly benign physical examination, including the absence of peritonitis, and imaging findings demonstrating extensive pneumatosis and mild pneumoperitoneum, which was suspected to be due to scant cyst rupture. Prior to formulating an operative plan, a computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained to evaluate for mesenteric ischemia, particularly given the patient’s history of atrial fibrillation. The CTA demonstrated increased pneumoperitoneum compared with the prior CT examination but revealed no evidence of vascular occlusion (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Real axial abdominal CT of a human patient showing diffuse free intraperitoneal gas (pneumoperitoneum) beneath the anterior abdominal wall, indicated by red arrows. The disease-focused article title (pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis) together with the caption and in-text phrase explicitly tying this pneumoperitoneum to PCI support attribution to the target disease; pneumoperitoneum from ruptured subserosal cysts is a recognized PCI manifestation. No exclusion criterion applies.

Intramural bowel gas with associated pneumoperitoneum is a classic CT presentation of PCI.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed an absence of parietal enhancement of the bowel, diffuse PI, and abundant HPVG. Gas was also present throughout the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. Additionally, an atheromatous obstruction was observed at the ostium of the superior mesenteric artery (Fig. 2). Refractory septic shock with disseminated intravascular coagulation precluded surgical treatment in this patient, and his condition rapidly deteriorated to multiorgan failure. He died 1 day later.

panels.rationale: Single-panel plain upright PA chest radiograph from a disease-focused case report of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis. The caption and in-text explicitly describe a large volume of bilateral sub-diaphragmatic free air (tension pneumoperitoneum), which matches the configured vocabulary finding pneumatosis_cystoides_intestinalis_free_intraperitoneal_gas (pneumoperitoneum from ruptured subserosal cysts; synonym subdiaphragmatic free air). The disease-focused article title together with the specific captioned manifestation supports attribution to pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis; prior caption triage also routed this as a real patient radiograph to keep. Free intraperitoneal air is a recognized less-common manifestation of PCI, so typicality is variant. No age, ethnicity, or skin findings are stated; no annotations are visible.

panels.figure_caption: Abdominal computed tomography scans illustrate the course of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis (PCI) in a patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with acarbose. The coronal view demonstrates characteristic findings of PCI, including a honeycomb-like cluster of air-filled cysts (black arrows) within the right colonic wall, along with notable accumulation of fecal material and gas throughout the colon (white arrows), and scattered free intraperitoneal gas (dashed arrows).
in_text_mentions: On physical examination, the abdomen was soft, and there were no elevated infection markers (Table 1). Computed tomography (CT) imaging of the abdomen revealed a distinctive honeycomb-like cluster of air-filled sacs within the right colonic wall, consistent with PCI. Additionally, scattered free gas was observed in the abdominal cavity, and multiple areas of fecal and gas accumulation were noted in the colon (Fig. 1, coronal image, arrow).

Multiple large “cysts” are seen within multiple loops of small bowel (dashed arrows), consistent with “pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis” seen in this patient with scleroderma.
in_text_mentions: Follow-up fluoroscopic J tube study the next day revealed irregular filling of the small bowel, suspicious for contrast extravasation outside of the small bowel lumen. Further confirmation by CT was performed which revealed endoluminal termination of jejunostomy catheter with no dissection of contrast into an intramural location, and note was made of worsening small bowel pneumatosis and pneumoperitoneum (Figures 2, 3 and 4). The patient was completely asymptomatic, treated conservatively with bowel rest and maintenance of fluids, and subsequently discharged home without surgical intervention.

panels.rationale: Single axial abdominal CT from a human patient. The panel-specific caption explicitly states 'pneumatosis intestinalis', and the in-text describes gas dissecting the sigmoid colon wall with a bulky pneumoperitoneum, directly attributing the image to the configured target disease. The visible intramural bowel gas and free intraperitoneal air match two vocabulary findings. No diagram, control, other-disease, or third-party issue is present.

in_text_mentions: tient presented with abdominal distention and fever. Complete blood count showed neutropenia. The patient received antibiotics and CT scans of the chest, abdomen, pelvis and sinuses were performed. Comparing with the initial scans, these images showed presence of gas dissecting the wall of sigmoid colon extending to the mesosigmoid, retroperitoneum and posterior mediastinum, and a bulky pneumoperitoneum without gas in the portal venous system. Moreover, there was the additional finding of a hematoma in the psoas major muscle associated with edema in the adjacent subcutaneous tissue (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT of a real patient from a case report of primary small-bowel pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis. The image shows a crescent of free intraperitoneal gas in the perihepatic space (indicated by the white arrow), directly attributed in both caption and in-text description to rupture of intramural gaseous cysts of PCI into the peritoneal cavity. This is a specific, visibly demonstrated manifestation of the configured target disease, matching the vocabulary finding for free intraperitoneal gas from ruptured subserosal cysts. No other disease, control, diagram or third-party material is involved.

panels.figure_caption: Abdominal CT scan showing free intraperitoneal air near the liver.
in_text_mentions: The onset of subobstructive symptoms over the following first month led the patient to repeat abdominal CT examination with intravenous contrast. It demonstrated the presence of small bowel PI with intraperitoneal free air near the liver and in the mesenteric fat due to the rupture of intramural gaseous cysts into the peritoneal cavity (Figure 3). A laparotomy was performed revealing some loops adherent to the parietal peritoneum due to earlier rupture of cysts with superimposed inflammation.

B: Axial contrast CT of the same patient; caption explicitly notes gas in the mesenteric veins (PVMG) in B/b in addition to intramural bowel gas. PMVG is a recognized accompaniment of pneumatosis intestinalis and is proposed as a finding since it is absent from the vocabulary. C: Coronal contrast CT reconstruction of the same patient showing extensive pneumatosis intestinalis; inset c with yellow arrow indicates the SMA embolism. Real patient image with a clear, captioned manifestation of the target disease. D: Coronal contrast CT of the same patient; caption explicitly describes gas in the portal veins of the left upper liver lobe (D/d) together with extensive PI. Portal venous gas is a...

plate_findings.evidence: multiple rounded and elevated, softened smooth-surfaced, mucosal lesions with foci of enanthem were found without loss of mucosal contiguity

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Left endoscopic panel shows the colon mucosa with multiple rounded, smooth-surfaced elevated lesions marked by red arrows, consistent with pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis pseudopolypoid blebs. panels.figure_caption: A 45-year-old female patient with a medical history of constipation and recurrent diverticulitis presented herself for an elective colonoscopy eight weeks after her last episode. These lesions were homogeneously distributed over the entire circumference of this intestinal segment. panels.figure_caption: Although the diagnosis can be made by radiological studies [3,4,5,6], a colorectal EUS and colonoscopy can be made in the same section without radiation and with high precision [4,5,6]. panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT panel showing curvilinear intramural gas in the jejunal wall (white arrows), a direct diagnostic manifestation of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis. The caption and in-text explicitly state the diagnosis of intestinal pneumatosis, and the triage confirms a real patient radiology image with no third-party restriction. The curvilinear intramural gas pattern on CT is a classic presentation; no free intraperitoneal air, portal venous gas, necrosis, or perforation is present, so only the intramural gas finding is tagged.

in_text_mentions: We repeated a colonoscopy and it revealed multiple polypoid formations of varying sizes (1-3 cm) in the ascending colon, covered by normal mucosa with superficial vessels (Figure 1), and diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon. After biopsy, the cysts collapsed and disappeared. Furthermore, only colon mucosa was found in the biopsy specimens (Figure 2). While X-ray film of the abdomen did not reveal any pathological findings, CT confirmed conspicuous gas bubbles in the ascending colon (Figure 3).

panels.figure_caption: Colonoscopy (A-B) Polypoid cysts with red overlying mucosa in the proximal sigmoid and distal descending colon. (C-D) Deflation of a 10mm polypoid lesion of the proximal sigmoid colon with cystic air bubbles.
in_text_mentions: A 51-year-old male with a past medical history of hypothyroidism presented for average-risk screening colonoscopy. The patient’s history was negative for smoking and alcohol consumption. During the colonoscopy, multiple polypoid cysts with red overlying mucosa were found in the proximal sigmoid and distal descending colon (Figure 1A-1B). Cystic air emerged with the biopsy of a benign 10 mm polypoid lesion in the proximal sigmoid colon (Figure 1C-1D). The patient was discharged with instructions for a computed tomography (CT) abdomen and pelvis with contrast at his next follow-up appointment.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Real patient colonoscopy of the descending colon showing numerous smooth, transparent, polypoid submucosal blebs — the classic endoscopic appearance of pneumatosis intestinalis, with the caption and in-text explicitly attributing the images to PI. B: Real patient colonoscopy showing a needle compressing/puncturing a submucosal gas-filled bleb in the descending colon, with subsequent collapse of the bubble — direct endoscopic evidence of pneumatosis intestinalis. C: Real patient colonoscopy showing multiple smooth, cystic, polypoid submucosal elevations in the descending colon — the classic endoscopic presentation of pneumatosis intestinalis. D: Real patient colonoscopy of the descending colon showing rounded, shiny, translucent submucosal blebs with overlying mucosal change — a classic endoscopic manifestation of pneumatosis intestinalis.

He received negative pressure drainage treatment with drainage tube in the higher-level hospital, and upgraded antibiotics to meropenem. panels.rationale: Single abdominal POCUS figure (no panel letters; treated as panel A) from a case report whose title and caption explicitly attribute the image to pneumatosis intestinalis. The caption states intramural air (yellow arrow) in the left upper quadrant of a 3-month-old, and the in-text describes sub-serosal echogenic foci suggestive of sonographic pneumatosis intestinalis. The image visibly shows echogenic intramural foci with yellow-arrow annotations, satisfying the intramural bowel gas finding. The coexisting doughnut/target sign reflects intussusception, which is noted only as a proposed finding since it is not a configured target disease. Real patient image, diagnostic quality, no third-party indication.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Autopsy gross specimen photograph of the colon from a human patient, opened to show numerous intramural gas-filled cystic spaces in the submucosa/muscularis propria - the gross correlate of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis. Real patient image, disease attribution certain from the PCI-focused article title and caption. B: Low-power histopathology (H&E upper, Masson trichrome lower) of human colon wall showing multilocular gas cysts occupying the submucosa and extending through the muscularis propria (M/SM, ICL, OLL labelled). Directly captioned and described as severe PCI on Fig. 1A-C; disease attribution certain. C: Masson trichrome histology of human colon showing a large intramural gas cyst dissecting between the inner circular layer (ICL) and outer longitudinal layer (OLL) of the muscularis propria. Part of Fig. 1A-C described as severe PCI spanning submucosa to muscularis propria; disease attribution clear. D: High-power H&E...

panels.rationale: Real patient colonoscopy image showing multiple smooth polypoid lesions covered by normal-appearing mucosa with superficial vessels in the ascending colon, the classic endoscopic appearance of submucosal gas cysts in pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis. The caption, in-text description (polypoid formations 1–3 cm covered by normal mucosa; cysts collapsed after biopsy), and the disease-focused case-report title ('Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis of the ascending colon related to acarbose treatment') all support attribution to pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis. The image overlay contains only endoscopy metadata (date, time, SCV-1, Comment), no diagnostic annotations. No age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or in-text.
panels.attribution_text: Vogel et al. Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis of the ascending colon related to acarbose treatment: a case report.. Journal of medical case reports 2009. doi:10.4076/1752-1947-3-9216. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Colonoscopy examination disclosed multiple polypoid lesions that were covered with inconspicuous mucosa with superficial vessels in the area of the ascending colon.
in_text_mentions: We repeated a colonoscopy and it revealed multiple polypoid formations of varying sizes (1-3 cm) in the ascending colon, covered by normal mucosa with superficial vessels (Figure 1), and diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon. After biopsy, the cysts collapsed and disappeared. Furthermore, only colon mucosa was found in the biopsy specimens (Figure 2). While X-ray film of the abdomen did not reveal any pathological findings, CT confirmed conspicuous gas bubbles in the ascending colon (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Intraoperative gross photograph from laparotomy showing a human patient's small intestine (jejunum and ileum) studded with widespread variable-sized serosal air cysts, the gross hallmark of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis. Caption and in-text both attribute these cysts to pneumatosis intestinalis and note they were intact without pneumoperitoneum or peritonitis. Arrows annotate the cysts. Real patient image, disease-specific manifestation, classic textbook presentation. [raw subtype: serosal]
panels.attribution_text: Saber. Pneumatosis intestinalis with complete remission: a case report.. Cases journal 2009. doi:10.1186/1757-1626-0002-0000007079. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: A photograph showing widespread variable sized serosal intestinal air cysts involving long segment of jejunum and ileum. All cysts were intact and were not incriminated as a cause of pneumoperitoneun or peritonitis.
in_text_mentions: After the routine work up and proper resuscitation, laparotomy was performed. Widespread variable sized serosal intestinal air cysts were seen at the first look involving long segment of jejunum and ileum. All cysts were intact and were not incriminated as a cause of pneumoperitoneun or peritonitis (Figure 1). Perforated duodenal ulcer, as the cause of generalized peritonitis, was repaired with direct closure and omental patch. Nothing was done for the intestinal air cysts. Metronidazol intravenous infusion was given two times daily.

panels.rationale: Abdominal CT figure (coronal reconstruction above, axial slice below) of a 7-year-old child from a case report whose title and caption center on pneumatosis intestinalis. Both views visibly demonstrate intramural gas outlining small-bowel loops, the hallmark CT manifestation of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis, and the in-text also attributes pneumoperitoneum and hepatic portal venous gas to this figure. Real human-patient radiology with no diagram, control, or third-party indicator; the captioned manifestation directly matches the configured target disease rather than the underlying tuberculosis.
panels.attribution_text: Alp et al. Abdominal tuberculosis in a child presenting with radiological evidence of pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas.. Journal of health, population, and nutrition 2010. doi:10.3329/jhpn.v28i6.6612. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Abdominal CT before treatment
in_text_mentions: a four-drug anti-tuberculosis regimen (streptomycin+isoniazid+rifampicin+pyrazinamide) was started. Over the first three weeks, clinical symptoms resolved, abdominal distention decreased, and he gained 2 kg in weight. After three weeks, abdominal CT showed a little improvement in the small-bowel pneumatosis, pneuperitoneum, and hepatic portal venous gas (Fig. 4 and 5). Because of his response to therapy (Fig. 6), he was discharged. However, two months after discharge from our hospital, we learned that he died suddenly at home. The cause of death was not known, and an autopsy was not performed.

in_text_mentions: A 56-year-old Swiss-born man who had recently developed abdominal pain and changes in his bowel habits underwent an optical colonoscopy. He was otherwise in good health and had no medical history other than a tendency to constipation. Colonoscopy revealed multiple submucosal polypoid lesions covered with normal mucosa in the colon. An abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan with a soft tissue window setting did not show any abnormal findings in the abdomen. CT colonography identified multiple submucosal gas cysts mostly located in the left colon (Figure 1A-C).

panels.rationale: Single coronal contrast-enhanced abdominal CT of a human patient. Caption and in-text explicitly localize pneumatosis intestinalis to the right lower quadrant (terminal ileum into the cecum), and the image shows a focal cluster of intramural gas-filled cysts in that region, matching the vocabulary finding for intramural bowel gas on CT. The figure belongs to an article on pneumatosis intestinalis in a patient with acute promyelocytic leukemia, but this panel itself depicts the bowel-wall gas manifestation, so it is attributed to pneumatosis_cystoides_intestinalis. No free intraperitoneal air is described. Orientation letters (R/I) and small mesenteric arrowhead markers are present.

The entire nodular area measures 8.4 × 3.5 × 2 cm. Upon sectioning, the nodules deflate and are consistent with air bubbles (a, b). Microscopically, the section of the colon showed multiple air-filled cystic structures located in the submucosa. The cysts were lined by macrophages and multinucleated giant cells with bland nuclei. No atypia, pleomorphism, or mitoses were identified. The overlying colonic mucosa exhibited mild reactive changes but did not show significant inflammation or adenomatous change (c)

panels.rationale: Single-panel gross autopsy photograph from an article whose title and in-text explicitly attribute the findings to pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis: the text describes multiple gas-filled cysts protruding through the colon wall, mesentery, and retroperitoneum, and states that air bubbles detected in the mediastinum (shown here) explain the pneumoperitoneum. The image visibly shows gas bubbles within retroperitoneal/mediastinal tissue at autopsy, a direct extraluminal manifestation of the same gas-cyst pathology of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis, so it qualifies as a real human-patient image of the target disease. The manifestation (gas dissecting to mediastinum/retroperitoneum rather than confined to the bowel wall) is a recognized but less common form, hence variant typicality. No ethnicity, age, or skin is shown.

in_text_mentions: onfirmed the situation of advanced cancer and the presence of multiple gas-filled cysts protruding through the colon wall, mesentery, and retroperitoneum. Unlike the surgical and CT scanning reports, the presence of air bubbles was also detected in the mediastinum, occupied by metastasis nodes in the pulmonary parenchyma (Figure 3), explaining the origin of pneumoperitoneum. After immunohistochemical study of cancer specimens by means of cytokeratin 18 and vimentin, the final diagnosis was carcinoma of thymus gland with sarcomatoid characteristic (T4N3aM1, IV stage in according with WHO 2004).

Intussusception is generally a disease that occurs in infants with loose fixation of the mesocolon, and adult cases are rare. Idiopathic intussusception in infants is more common (75%), and only 25% of cases are due to a pathological lead point (PLP). In adults, PLPs, such as a tumor or Meckel's diverticulum, have been reported in 90% of cases. 7 In this case, the PCI in combination with a mucosal defect found therein (Figure 2c) was considered the likely PLP for the patient's intussusception.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Coronal CT panel from a case report on pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis; the caption specifically identifies free intraperitoneal gas, an allowed PCI finding (pneumoperitoneum from ruptured subserosal cysts). The free gas is less specific than intramural gas, hence variant typicality and slightly lower confidence. B: Axial CT panel directly shows gas bubbles in the intestinal wall and mesentery, the classic intramural gas manifestation of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis, supported by the panel-specific caption and the disease-focused article title.

plate_findings.evidence: In-text: 'In mucosal microgranular areas, scattered microvacuoles ... were present, suggesting PI'; visual clear microvacuolated spaces within the cecal mucosa on HE.
In-text: 'microvacuoles with or without foreign-body reaction'; visual histiocytic/giant-cell-type cells lining and surrounding the clear spaces.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Autopsy hematoxylin-eosin section of cecal mucosa from the reported pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis case. It shows scattered microvacuoles (submucosal gas cysts) with foreign-body/giant-cell reaction together with erosive lymphocytic changes, matching the in-text statement that the microgranular mucosal areas suggested PI. Real human-patient histology directly attributable to the configured disease. B: Immunohistochemical CD8 stain of the same erosive cecal mucosa at autopsy (Fig. 5 per in-text: CD8+ lymphocytes infiltrated crypts and lamina mucosae of the darkly reddish erosive areas). It is a real human-patient section from the PCI case; the CD8 signal characterizes the immune infiltrate of the pneumatosis-affected erosive mucosa rather than the gas cysts themselves, so it is included with moderate confidence and the CD8 finding is proposed rather than drawn from the PCI vocabulary.

Darkly reddish areas showed mucosal erosion, in which immunohistochemically CD8+ lymphocytes infiltrated crypts and lamina mucosae (Fig. 5). In mucosal microgranular areas, scattered microvacuoles with or without foreign-body reaction were present, suggesting PI. Caption explicitly attributes the findings to pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis: intramural small-bowel gas cysts (dashed arrow) and pneumoperitoneum anterior to the liver (arrow), matching the disease-focused article title. No age, ethnicity, or skin assessment applicable; scleroderma is an underlying condition, not a PCI subtype, so subtype is null.
panels.attribution_text: Devgun and Hassan. Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis: a rare benign cause of pneumoperitoneum.. Case reports in radiology 2013. doi:10.1155/2013/353245. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Axial CT image with enteric contrast demonstrates pneumoperitoneum in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen, anterior to the liver (arrow). Multiple large “cysts” are seen within the wall of the small bowel (dashed arrow), consistent with “pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis” seen in this patient with scleroderma. Contrast is noted in a loop of small bowel at the left side, without extravasation of contrast from the small bowel.
in_text_mentions: Follow-up fluoroscopic J tube study the next day revealed irregular filling of the small bowel, suspicious for contrast extravasation outside of the small bowel lumen. Further confirmation by CT was performed which revealed endoluminal termination of jejunostomy catheter with no dissection of contrast into an intramural location, and note was made of worsening small bowel pneumatosis and pneumoperitoneum (Figures 2, 3 and 4). The patient was completely asymptomatic, treated conservatively with bowel rest and maintenance of fluids, and subsequently discharged home without surgical intervention.

in_text_mentions: One month later, presenting with a new episode of generalized abdominal pain, the patient underwent abdominal ultrasound (US) and plain abdominal film. The latter showed a large amount of intramural gas within some small bowel loops (Figure 1); US was useless due to intestinal tympanites. Abdominal CT with intravenous contrast administration was performed further to evaluate the pneumatosis and to investigate any possible complications. The scans confirmed the presence of small gas-filled cysts arising from the wall of the jejunum and ileum (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Axial CT of the abdomen in a patient from a case report of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis (occurring as a complication of granulomatosis with polyangiitis); yellow arrows indicate extensive intramural bowel wall gas with additional mesenteric and abdominal wall gas, a classic CT presentation of PCI. Free intraperitoneal air is only an unexcluded possibility ('difficult, however, to rule out') and portomesenteric pneumatosis is explicitly stated as not detected, so neither is tagged as a finding. b: Coronal CT reformat of the same patient with pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis from the case report; yellow arrows show the same extensive intramural bowel wall gas with mesenteric and abdominal wall involvement, confirming the axial findings. As in panel (a), free air is only an unexcluded possibility and portomesenteric pneumatosis is explicitly excluded, so only intramural bowel gas is tagged from the vocabulary.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Coronal CT of the abdomen and pelvis showing extensive bubble-like pneumatosis intestinalis along the entire colon (white arrows), the classic CT presentation of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis in a human patient; directly supported by the caption and in-text mentions of PI extending from the ascending colon to the rectum. B: Axial CT showing branching lucencies of hepatic portal venous gas and a low-attenuation right hepatic lobe lesion suggestive of infarction (black arrows) in the same patient with pneumatosis intestinalis; the article title directly links portal venous gas with pneumatosis intestinalis, and the in-text describes these findings alongside the colonic pneumatosis, supporting attribution to the disease spectrum.

panels.figure_caption: Computed tomography (CT) image of the abdomen and pelvis. The CT scan shows extensive bubble-like pneumatosis intestinalis along the entire colon (A, white arrows), branching lucencies indicating hepatic portal venous gas, and a low-attenuation lesion in the right lobe of the liver, suggestive of infarction of the liver (B, black arrows).
in_text_mentions: omental dirty fat infiltration had all markedly decreased. However, PI extending from the ascending colon to the rectum was detected in the absence of pneumoperitoneum or other abnormalities (Figure 3A). Moreover, a large volume of hepatic PVG and a low-attenuation lesion in the right lobe of the liver were observed. These findings were considered to be suggestive of an infarction of the liver (Figure 3B). Although the CT images were striking, surgical exploration was not performed since the patient was non-toxic and had mild symptoms. The patient was not taking any medicine except gefitinib.

panels.rationale: Single CT image from a case report on pneumatosis intestinalis. The caption identifies a transition point in the mid-descending colon, and the linked in-text mention states the transverse colon was distended with pneumatosis. The panel is a real patient CT and supports pneumatosis_cystoides_intestinalis via intramural gas/pneumatosis, though the caption itself emphasizes the transition point rather than the gas cysts.
